title: An infinite system has no maximum in an HF-ordering and every element lies below a product
source_title: The elementary theory of free Steiner triple systems

proof_spans.label: the complete author proof of the labelled lemma, retained line for line

standard_prerequisites.name: HF-ordering of an infinite system
standard_prerequisites.statement: A linear ordering in which each element has at most one pair of smaller elements forming a block with it.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is the ordering under consideration in both items.

standard_prerequisites.name: Block
standard_prerequisites.statement: A block is a triple of elements closed under the partial operation of the Steiner triple system.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what the maximality argument counts.

standard_prerequisites.name: Infinite Steiner triple system
standard_prerequisites.statement: The system has more than three elements, so each element lies in several blocks.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is what makes the first item work.

core_obligations: For the first item, assume the ordering has a maximum and use that the element lies in two distinct blocks, whose other members are all below it by maximality, to contradict the defining condition of an HF-ordering (source line 836).

For the second item, assume the opposite and take b above a such that every block through a has a member at most b; choose b1 and b2 above b with their product below the larger of them, which is possible by the first item (source line 838).
Derive from that configuration a block whose two smaller members form a block with a larger element, contradicting the HF property (source line 838).

proof_roadmap.step: First item by counting the blocks through a purported maximum.
Second item by finding a suitable pair above b and reaching a contradiction.

difficulty_reason: Counted unit is the author's labelled lemma at source lines 829-834, which has two items: an HF-ordering of an infinite Steiner triple system has no maximum, and below every product decomposition of a there are two elements above any prescribed b. The proof (source lines 835-839) argues differently for the two items. The first counts the two blocks through a supposed maximum: since the system has more than three elements both other members of those blocks are below it, and the two blocks then witness the failure of the HF condition. The second is a contradiction argument that first chooses a pair above b using the first item and then reads off a violation of the HF property. The statement records the two conclusions and neither the block counting nor the construction of the pair.
